name: Ouroboros ClaimBand Compliance Anklet MK-3
description: A matte-black polycarbonate band, roughly 28mm wide, locked around the ankle with a tamper-evident ceramic pin seal. The outer face displays a faint amber pulse every four seconds — the Ouroboros risk-management logo barely visible under a scratch-resistant film worn smooth from months of daily contact. Issued in two flavors: court-mandated (orange pulse) and voluntary employer-bonding compliance (blue pulse), though both models are physically identical. Street-modified versions circulate on the Gray Zone with the pulse spoofed green to mimic parole clearance.
functionality: Continuous geo-tracking with 10-meter accuracy, biometric pulse monitoring, tamper-alert triggering silent corpsec notification. Voluntary bonding versions unlock transit subsidies and employer housing credits. Cannot be removed without a licensed Ouroboros compliance terminal.
what_it_says: You owe someone something — whether that's the courts, your employer, or a debt broker depends entirely on the pulse color.
worn_by: Tier 1 residents on supervised resettlement programs
Tier 2 workers under employer bonding agreements
people with spoofed units passing checkpoints
price_range: Φ0 (court-issued) / Φ180–Φ340 (employer-bond voluntary) / Φ60–Φ90 (spoofed street unit)
story_hooks: A character discovers their 'voluntary' employer-bond anklet has the same firmware as a court-ordered unit — meaning Ouroboros was tracking them before they ever signed anything.
A the Gray Zone fixer sells spoofed green-pulse units; one bad batch has a delayed tamper flag that fires twelve hours after installation, right in the middle of a job.
A Tier 3 mid-manager finds an Ouroboros compliance terminal in a maintenance closet — and realizes it can remove anklets without logging the removal.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian ankle-worn band that reads as institutional restraint—sleek but oppressive. The matte-black polymer has a quasi-medical aesthetic that sits between penal hardware and biometric monitoring device. On-person, it creates a visual anchor point that draws the eye downward, signaling control and surveillance regardless of the wearer's tier.
physical_description.fit: Snug circumferential fit around the ankle with minimal adjustment tolerance. Designed for security, not comfort—the band sits flush against skin with no flex or give. The 28mm width is substantial enough to be visible even under loose pant legs.
physical_description.primary_material: Matte-black polycarbonate; tamper-evident ceramic locking pin with polymer sheath
physical_description.texture: Smooth, scratch-resistant outer film worn to a dull finish from repetitive contact with skin and clothing. The ceramic seal has a slightly raised tactile edge. Under harsh light, micro-abrasions catch like scars on dark ice.
physical_description.color_scheme: Matte black primary with amber, orange, or blue pulse-indicator light cycling every four seconds beneath a worn protective film. Black-market variants sport spoofed green pulses. The branding (Ouroboros serpent symbol) is deliberately subtle, almost subliminal.
physical_description.closures: Permanent ceramic pin-lock seal with tamper-detection—not designed for user removal. Street rumors suggest plasma cutters and electromagnetic pulse tools exist to bypass; official removal requires authorized LoopCell technician or court order.
distinctive_features: Embedded LED pulse-indicator (color-coded by status: orange=court-mandated, blue=employer-voluntary, green=street-spoofed)
Tamper-evident ceramic seal that fractures visibly if removal is attempted
Scratch-resistant film overlay protecting the Ouroboros logo
Minimal weight design to reduce friction and skin irritation during extended wear
Court-issue versions often bear scuffed date stamps or registry codes on the inner surface
Real-time biometric uplink capability (pulse, temperature, location broadcast)
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3–5 marker. Tier 1–2 corpo employees rarely wear them; when they do, it signals legal liability or voluntary corporate wellness programs (coded as 'voluntary bonding'). Street presence indicates either systemic surveillance (court mandate) or economic desperation (employer condition for work access). Tier 5 wearing a spoofed green variant is high-risk—visible false compliance.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing one marks the wearer as legally monitored, debt-bonded to an employer, or under rehabilitation contract. The pulse color broadcasts status to anyone reading the street—orange is state control, blue is corpo-debt, green is either freedom or lies. In some GLMZ subcultures, modified bands are worn as anti-establishment statement jewelry, intentionally misrepresenting status.
physical_description.condition_typical: Worn units show polished patches from ankle movement, faded logos under the film, and micro-cracks around the seal from attempted tampering. Long-term wearers develop calluses visible around the band's edges. Court-mandated versions accumulate minor cosmetic damage; employer-issue bands are often swapped out quarterly and therefore cleaner.
